sections.Learning objectives: The student knows and understands the information required to design and conduct experimental investigations in the laboratory or wind tunnel; He/she is able to acquire knowledge independently concerning the principles and applications of innovative techniques in the field of fluid dynamics which have been successfully developed in recent years; Is able to analyse, interpret and critically evaluate the results of experiments with independent judgement; He/she is able to find the necessary information to tackle new problems and to design the experiment as a whole according to the investigation and the results to be obtained.
sections.Prerequisites: It is advisable to have passed the Fluid Mechanics exam.
sections.Course unit content: The course aims to provide students with the tools to study the interaction between wind and the bodies it impacts. Models of wind generation and characteristics are analysed on the basis of the physics of the atmosphere, with a description of the statistics used to describe the random velocity field that develops in the Earth's atmospheric boundary layer. The fluid-dynamic aspects induced by the presence of bodies immersed in the fluid vein of elongated or squat geometry are then analysed, defining the fundamental parameters governing the physical phenomenon. The similarity criteria adopted for wind tunnel modelling are introduced, with a description of the different types of wind tunnels. The measuring instruments used are introduced and described. Finally, the analytical and numerical models most frequently adopted in CFD are introduced.

sections.Learning objectives: At the end of the course the student will have acquired - knowledge relating to the design of the experimentation (even virtual) on Energy Systems and the interpretation of the obtained results; - skills concerning the numerical and experimental characterization of Energy Systems operations; - tools for the implementation, execution and analysis of models for the simulation of Energy Systems and for the interpretation of simulation results.
sections.Prerequisites: A basic knowledge of fundamentals of Mathematics, Physics Thermodynamics, Fluid Mechanics and Energy Systems is required.
sections.Course unit content: The course is a complement to the theoretical contents presented in the Energy Systems AB (I Module) course, which is held in the first semester. During the course, energy conversion systems (turbogas, steam plants and internal combustion engines) and their components will be analyzed with IT tools in order to determine their performance as the operating conditions vary. The main problems related to the experimental characterization of energy systems and fluid machines will also be analysed in this framework.
sections.Full programme: The course is divided into two parts. The first part analyzes the equipment required for experimentation, with a particular focus on the instruments and sensors typically used in test cells, the measurements acquired, and signal processing. Emphasis is placed on the procedures needed to perform test‑bench experiments under both steady‑state and transient conditions. The second part of the course focuses on the use of virtual environments for the simulation and modeling of energy systems. Specifically, several exercises will be proposed to numerically solve engineering problems through physical–mathematical modeling (calculation of thermodynamic transformations, analysis of energy systems). The models developed will then be used to investigate the effect of the main control parameters on system performance; in this way, students will be able to understand their impact through virtual experimentation of the system under study. These data will subsequently be used to generate reports that clearly and technically present the results of the analyses performed.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of this course the student should know the basics of machine design. He should gain understanding of the many factors affecting the design of mechanical parts with special regards to safety and reliability. He should be familiar with design schemes and checks required to analyze machine parts. Applying knowledge and understanding: He should be able to design a mechanical part on the basis of suitable material and process selection, load analysis and functional requirements. He should be able to select from catalogues the main mechanical components found in machines. He should be able to draw and dimension the part for production. Making judgments: By the end of the course the student should be able to critically analyze machines and mechanical components and to their functions and requisites. Communication skills: The student should be able to clearly present the functioning of mechanical devices and the design issues involved.
sections.Prerequisites: It will be very useful to recall the following concepts: - Physics 1: units of measurement, forces and moments in a plane, vector representation, graphical resolution of static equilibrium - Machine drawing: views, dimensioning, dimensional and geometric tolerances, bearing assembly - Mechanical technology: machining technologies, heat treatment of steel - Metallurgy: metal alloys and their applications, mechanical testing - Structural science: beam theory, mass geometry, de Saint-Venant theory - Rational mechanics: kinematics, rigid body dynamics, kinematic mechanisms, and force calculations
sections.Course unit content: The course covers the principles of mechanical design applied to machine components, starting with the strength characteristics of commonly used materials and the concept of safety. It then introduces methods and models for the schematization of acting loads and the calculation and sizing of components. A key aspect is the introduction to strength testing under fatigue loads.
sections.Full programme: Introduction to Construction Design, Safety, Factor of Safety with Statistical Reliability Concepts, Technical Standards, Mechanical Testing of Materials, Tensile, Hardness, Impact, Fatigue, Fracture Testing, Metallic Materials (Steel, Cast Iron, Aluminum, Magnesium, Titanium Alloys), Non-Metallic Materials (Polymers and Ceramics), Manufacturing Technologies, Selection Criteria. Load Analysis, Equilibrium, Application of the Beam Model in Mechanics, Normal Force, Bending, Shear, and Torsion. Stresses and Strains. Mohr Circles. Principal Stresses, Strength Criteria (Tresca, Von Mises, Rankine), Ductility and Brittleness. Compressive Buckling and Eulerian Loading. Stiffness. Highly Curvatured Beams. Notched Geometries, Nominal and Local Stresses, Stress Concentration Factor Kt. Conformal and Non-Conformal Contact, Specific Contact Pressure, Hertzian Theory, Stresses in Contact between Elementary Bodies. Thermal Expansion. Fatigue of Metallic Materials, Characteristics of the Phenomenon, Fatigue Testing, Stress Limit fatigue, S/N curves, fatigue parameter estimates, influence factors, mean stress effect, fatigue damage accumulation, multiaxial stress effect, notch sensitivity, Notch effect factor Kf. Contact fatigue, pitting, fretting.
sections.Bibliography: - Lecture slides - Shigley - Progetto e costruzione di macchine, MCGraw-Hill -Beer, et al., Meccanica dei solidi, MCGraw-Hill
sections.Teaching methods: Course topics are presented through lectures and numerical exercises carried out in the classroom. Problems are proposed to be carried out at home with subsequent discussion in the classroom. Groups of students are also stimulated to analyse and study a real mechanical device.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The examination consists of a written test, which must be passed with a minimum score of 18/30, followed by an oral test. In the written exam, students will be required to solve an exercise concerning the design of a simple mechanical system, such as a lifting device, a pressure vessel or a drive shaft, considering the main factors that determine the safety of the system, such as the choice of the most suitable materials, durability, or compliance with regulations. In order to pass the written exam, it is essential to correctly perform the load analysis by means of static resolution and the determination of internal actions. In the oral exam, two theoretical topics are usually given for discussion, and a request may be made for an analysis of the failure of a mechanical component such as a spring, a drive shaft or a gear, for which possible improvements must also be provided. The final mark will be the sum of the marks for the two tests; admission to the oral exam may be granted with a mark of 17 with an asterisk, which means that a good oral performance is expected given the extreme criticality of the written exam. This exam structure is reserved for students whose study plan includes only Module I (Machine Construction A, 6 credits), while for students who opt for Module II (Machine Construction AB, 12 credits), i.e. for the Design curriculum, learning will be assessed in a single final examination for Module II, for which it is (obviously) essential to be able to solve the exercises in Module I. sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and ability to understand: (I Dublin Descriptor) By the end of the course, the student will have developed and integrated his or her basic knowledge of metallic materials suitable for component fabrication using foundry and additive manufacturing technologies. He/she will have gained awareness of issues related to physical metallurgy, relationships between microstructure and mechanical properties of ferrous and non-ferrous alloys. In particular, by the end of the course the student will be able to select appropriate materials and heat treatments for engineering design. Skills: (II Descriptor: Ability to apply knowledge and understanding) Through lessons and in-class exercises related to all program topics, the student will learn how to apply the knowledge gained in a design context. Autonomy of judgment: (III, IV, V Dublin descriptor) The student should be able to critically understand the characteristics and behavior of matter by evaluating its properties and suitability in relation to the intended applications. He/she will also have to process the relevant data to verify the required performance. Communication skills: (III, IV, V Dublin descriptor) At the end of the course the student should have acquired sufficient language skills, at least as regards the specific technological terminology of the teachings.
sections.Full programme: Basic knowledge of physical metallurgy: Brief introduction to crystallography. Diffusion phenomena correlated to the main heat treatments: I° and II° Fick’s law. Defects within the metallic materials. Phase diagrams: basic characteristics, lever rule, cooling pathways at the thermodynamic equilibrium. Phase diagram of Fe-Fe3C and microstructures. Strengthening mechanisms of the metallic materials. Solidification in conventional and innovative processes. Mechanical characterisation: Tensile test, hardness test, and Charpy impact test. Innovative production process: Metal additive manufacturing: general description, applications and operation of the machine. Process parameters. Advantages and Disadvantages. Steel: Designation. The main microstructures obtained during the main industrial heat treatments. Heat treatments: quenching, annealing, tempering, normalizing. Nitriding and carburizing. Brief description of structural steels, special structural steels, tool steels, and stainless steels. Aluminium alloys: Designations. Main aluminium alloys: microstructure, mechanical properties and applications. Production of aluminium. Main heat treatments and effects induced by cold deformation. Additive Manufacturing. Analysis of application cases and selection criteria for metallic materials: During the course, various application cases will be presented, in which the selection of metallic materials will be carried out based on the required mechanical properties, the component’s function, and the choice of suitable treatments to meet specific operating conditions at room and high temperatures.

sections.Learning objectives: On the basis of a deep knowledge of kinematics, statics and dynamics of mechanical system, the course provides the practical and theorical knowledge required for a proper functional design of machines and their devices.
sections.Prerequisites: Meccanica razionale
sections.Course unit content: Mechanisms assembly. Forces acting on mechanisms. Fundamental concepts of tribology: friction, wearing, lubrication Joints, brakes, clutches. Concepts of kinematics and dynamics and applications to mechanisms. Gears. Transmissions.
sections.Full programme: Historical notes and terminology. Degrees of freedom, Gruebler's and Kutzbach's formulas. Friction: sliding and static friction; cases of friction in prismatic, revolute, thrust, inclined plane, screw-nut pairs; brakes and clutches; rolling friction; cases of idler, driving, and driven wheels; vehicle examples; efficiency, machines in series and in parallel, retrograde motion. Lubrication: Newtonian fluids, mass conservation, constitutive laws, viscosity and units of measurement, Reynolds equation in 2D and 3D, introduction to elastohydrodynamics; hydrodynamic lubrication: applications – fixed and tilting-pad bearings (axial and radial), bushings, Sommerfeld number; hydrostatic lubrication. Kinematics: Galileo’s theorem, instantaneous center of rotation, trajectories, centroids and polodes, Euler-Savary theorem, conjugate profiles, inflection circle, Rivals’ theorem, applications. Linkage systems: analysis and synthesis of four-bar and six-bar linkages, slider-crank mechanisms, Roberts’ theorem, Oldham coupling, Cardan joint, brief notes on other joints (Birfield, tripod, Rzeppa). Cam mechanisms and motion laws. Gears: friction wheels and motivation for toothed gears, involute curve and its properties, pinion and rack, involute spur gears. Chain and belt transmissions. Dynamics of slider-crank mechanisms, substitution masses, balancing of engines with 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 12 cylinders.

sections.Learning objectives: The integrated course provides knowledge and skills to understand the operating principles, real characteristics, and performance of major energy systems and prime movers (gas turbines, internal combustion engines, steam plants). By the end of the course, students will be able to: - Understand the fundamentals of energy conversion and the types of fluid machines (drivers and driven). - Analyze real thermodynamic transformations and calculate performance parameters (efficiency, specific fuel consumption). - Assess energy system performance under varying operating conditions. - Critically compare different plant configurations and select fluid machines for specific applications. - Present evaluations and comparisons effectively using graphical and numerical representations.
sections.Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of: - Calculus - Physics - Thermodynamics - Fluid Mechanics - Applied Thermodynamics
sections.Course unit content: - Conventional and renewable energy sources. - Energy systems and fluid machines: types, classification, and components. - Steam plants, gas turbine plants, reciprocating internal combustion engines. - Combined-cycle and cogeneration systems. - Ideal, limiting, and real thermodynamic cycles (Rankine, Joule, Otto, Diesel, Sabathé). - Analysis of real thermodynamic transformations and performance calculations. - Fluid flow in ducts, compression and expansion processes, sonic conditions. - Fluid machines: pumps, compressors, fans, turbines. - Renewable energy conversion: hydroelectric, photovoltaic, bioenergy systems. - Overview of energy cost and utilization factor.
sections.Full programme: - Energy demand, sources, and conversion processes. - Thermodynamic fundamentals: mass and energy balances, ideal gas transformations, property calculations. - Hydrocarbon combustion: stoichiometric air calculation, calorific values. - Thermodynamic cycles: ideal, limiting, and real; work and heat exchange calculations. - Gas turbine plants: components, cycle variants, Joule cycle optimization. - Steam plants: ideal and real cycles, regeneration, reheating, boilers, condensers, cooling towers. - Internal combustion engines: ideal and real cycles, losses, supercharging, performance curves. - Combined-cycle and cogeneration systems: performance indices (IRE, PES). - Renewable energy conversion: hydroelectric systems, photovoltaic systems, bioenergy. - Fluid machines: classification, similarity laws, characteristic curves, cavitation, compressors, fans. - Quantitative analysis of performance and thermodynamic parameters.

sections.Learning objectives: This module aims to provide in-depth knowledge and skills (i.e., the ability to apply knowledge) necessary to assess the real-world operating characteristics and performance of energy systems, with particular emphasis on most commonly used the power plants (gas turbines, Internal Combustion Engines, and steam plants). To develop deeper skills in assessing the performance of any thermal power plant for energy generation and conversion, students are required to demonstrate the achievement of the following objectives by the end of the module. Knowledge and understanding: At the end of the course, students will be able to understand the real operating characteristics and performance of power generation systems and the main prime movers used today. They will also have acquired specific knowledge for assessing real thermodynamic transformations, for calculating thermodynamic parameters and heat and work exchanges with reference to real cases. They will therefore be familiar with the problems, limitations, advantages, and disadvantages of the considered power plants and their main components in real operating conditions. Applying knowledge and understanding: The student will be able to calculate the performance parameters of engines, with particular reference to efficiency and specific fuel consumption. They will also be able to define the behavior of real thermodynamic transformations occurring in power plants and their components in order to qualitatively and quantitatively evaluate the thermodynamic states and real transormations, as well as identify solutions to improve performance. Making judgments: The student will have tools and knowledge needed to critically evaluate and compare different solutions for implementing real energy conversion processes in power systems, taking into account thereal behavior of transformations and processes, while also considering possible alternatives. Communication skills: The student will gain the tools required to effectively present evaluations and comparisons of different solutions for implementing energy conversion processes in power plants, through both graphical and numerical representations of the real thermodynamic transformations and cycles, as well as the main performance parameters commonly used. Learning skills: Using the knowledge acquired in the course, students will be able to independently get information, characteristics, and technical data on Energy Systems that can be studied and/or available on the market, thus improving own skills on the solutions proposed and/or applied for the implementation and management of Energy Systems.
sections.Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of fundamentals of Mathematics, Physics, Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics is required.
sections.Course unit content: Energy Systems and Fluid Machines: classification and components. Review of Thermodynamics. Fundamental equations: mass and energy conservation; momentum and moment of momentum equations. Application to fluid flow in fixed and moving channels. Ideal, Limit, and Real thermodynamic cycles. Overview of Energy costs and utilization factors. Compressible Fluid Machines. Compression and expansion processes on thermodynamic diagrams; compression and expansion efficiencies. Total and stagnation quantities. Fluid Flow in fixed channels: converging channels, converging-diverging channels. Velocity and pressure trends, sonic and choking conditions. Steam Engines. Real Cycles: thermodynamic transformations in real Rankine cycles with saturated and superheated steam; performance calculation for reheated and regenerated steam plants in real operation. Steam generators: types and schemes; efficiency. Superheaters and economizers. Air preheaters. Condenser and cooling towers. Reciprocating internal combustion engines (ICEs). Limit thermodynamic cycles: an overview of calculation methodology. Real thermodynamic cycles: trends of real transformations and main causes of deviation from the ideal case. Indicated cycle and calculation of effective power in internal combustion engines. Mean effective pressure. Volumetric efficiency. Overview of combustion processes. Air and fuel supply processes in ICEs. Mechanical supercharging and turbocharging. Characteristic curves. Gas turbines: thermodynamic processes in the Joule cycle in the limit and real cases. Real thermodynamic cycles on the (h, s) and (T, s) diagrams; effective specific work, effective power, and thermodynamic efficiency in limit and real Joule cycle. Effect of compression ratio and maximum cycle temperature. Turbine inlet temperature (TIT) and air-fuel ratio: effects on efficiency. Optimization of the real Joule cycle with reference to specific work and efficiency.
sections.Full programme: Energy Systems and Fluid Machines: characteristics and classification. Internal and External Combustion Plants. Components of Energy Systems. Thermodynamics reminders: closed and open systems, Heat Exchangers and Fluid Machinery. Fundamental equations: mass and energy conservation; momentum and moment of momentum equations. Application of conservation equations to fluid flow in fixed and moving channels. Thermodynamic cycles and pseudo-cycles: thermodynamic transformations, work and heat exchange calculation. Ideal, Limit, and Real Cycles. Overview on energy cost and utilization coefficient. Compressible Fluid Machines. Compression and expansion transformations on thermodynamic diagrams; real and ideal transformations. Compression and expansion efficiencies, recovery and counter-recovery phenomena. Intercooled and post-combustion compression. total and stagnation quantities. Fluid flow in fixed-wall ducts: converging ducts, converging-diverging ducts. Evaluation of velocity and pressure trends with a 1-D approach. Sonic and choking conditions. Valves and pressure reducers. Notes on fluid flow in moving channels. Steam power plants: overview of the most common system configurations. Real cycles for steam power plants: transformations in real Rankine cycles with saturated and superheated steam. Regeneration and reheating: real thermodynamic cycles on the (h, s) and (T, s) diagrams. Performance calculation of simple, reheated, and regenerated steam power plants in real situations. Steam generators: types and basic schemes. Steam generator efficiency: direct and indirect calculations. Superheaters and economizers. Air preheaters. The condenser and cooling towers. The deaerator. Reciprocating internal combustion engines (ICEs). Review of operating principles and fundamental components. Limit thermodynamic cycles: an overview of calculation methodology. Real thermodynamic cycles: evolution of real transformations and main causes of deviation from the ideal case. Time losses, heat exchange, pressure drops through intake and exhaust valves and throttle valve. Indicated cycle and calculation of effective power in ICE. Mean effective pressure. Volumetric efficiency. Overview of combustion processes in spark-ignition and Diesel engines. Air and fuel supply processes in ICEs: intake and exhaust systems and polar diagram of ideal and real valves timing. Mechanical supercharging and turbocharging. Characteristic curves of internal combustion engines. Gas turbines: an overview of the most common configurations. Real cycles for gas turbine power plants: thermodynamic transformations in the Joule cycle in the limit and real cases. Real thermodynamic cycles on the (h, s) and (T, s) diagrams. Calculation of effective specific work, effective power, and thermodynamic efficiency in limit and real Joule cycle. Effect of compression ratio and maximum cycle temperature. Calculation of turbine inlet temperature (TIT) and air-fuel ratio values: effects on efficiency and problems arising from material resistance. Introduction to blade cooling. Introduction to combustion chamber geometry. Optimization of the real Joule cycle with reference to specific work and efficiency.

title: MACHINE DESIGN A
discipline: Progettazione meccanica e costruzione di macchine (ING-IND/14)

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of this course the student should know the basics of machine design. He should gain understanding of the many factors affecting the design of mechanical parts with special regards to safety and reliability. He should be familiar with design schemes and checks required to analyze machine parts. Applying knowledge and understanding: He should be able to design a mechanical part on the basis of suitable material and process selection, load analysis and functional requirements. He should be able to select from catalogues the main mechanical components found in machines. He should be able to draw and dimension the part for production. Making judgments: By the end of the course the student should be able to critically analyze machines and mechanical components and to their functions and requisites. Communication skills: The student should be able to clearly present the functioning of mechanical devices and the design issues involved.
sections.Prerequisites: It will be very useful to recall the following concepts: - Physics 1: units of measurement, forces and moments in a plane, vector representation, graphical resolution of static equilibrium - Machine drawing: views, dimensioning, dimensional and geometric tolerances, bearing assembly - Mechanical technology: machining technologies, heat treatment of steel - Metallurgy: metal alloys and their applications, mechanical testing - Structural science: beam theory, mass geometry, de Saint-Venant theory - Rational mechanics: kinematics, rigid body dynamics, kinematic mechanisms, and force calculations
sections.Course unit content: The course covers the principles of mechanical design applied to machine components, starting with the strength characteristics of commonly used materials and the concept of safety. It then introduces methods and models for the schematization of acting loads and the calculation and sizing of components. A key aspect is the introduction to strength testing under fatigue loads.
sections.Full programme: Introduction to Construction Design, Safety, Factor of Safety with Statistical Reliability Concepts, Technical Standards, Mechanical Testing of Materials, Tensile, Hardness, Impact, Fatigue, Fracture Testing, Metallic Materials (Steel, Cast Iron, Aluminum, Magnesium, Titanium Alloys), Non-Metallic Materials (Polymers and Ceramics), Manufacturing Technologies, Selection Criteria. Load Analysis, Equilibrium, Application of the Beam Model in Mechanics, Normal Force, Bending, Shear, and Torsion. Stresses and Strains. Mohr Circles. Principal Stresses, Strength Criteria (Tresca, Von Mises, Rankine), Ductility and Brittleness. Compressive Buckling and Eulerian Loading. Stiffness. Highly Curvatured Beams. Notched Geometries, Nominal and Local Stresses, Stress Concentration Factor Kt. Conformal and Non-Conformal Contact, Specific Contact Pressure, Hertzian Theory, Stresses in Contact between Elementary Bodies. Thermal Expansion. Fatigue of Metallic Materials, Characteristics of the Phenomenon, Fatigue Testing, Stress Limit fatigue, S/N curves, fatigue parameter estimates, influence factors, mean stress effect, fatigue damage accumulation, multiaxial stress effect, notch sensitivity, Notch effect factor Kf. Contact fatigue, pitting, fretting.

sections.Teaching methods: Course topics are presented through lectures and numerical exercises carried out in the classroom. Problems are proposed to be carried out at home with subsequent discussion in the classroom. Groups of students are also stimulated to analyse and study a real mechanical device.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The examination consists of a written test, which must be passed with a minimum score of 18/30, followed by an oral test. In the written exam, students will be required to solve an exercise concerning the design of a simple mechanical system, such as a lifting device, a pressure vessel or a drive shaft, considering the main factors that determine the safety of the system, such as the choice of the most suitable materials, durability, or compliance with regulations. In order to pass the written exam, it is essential to correctly perform the load analysis by means of static resolution and the determination of internal actions. In the oral exam, two theoretical topics are usually given for discussion, and a request may be made for an analysis of the failure of a mechanical component such as a spring, a drive shaft or a gear, for which possible improvements must also be provided. The final mark will be the sum of the marks for the two tests; admission to the oral exam may be granted with a mark of 17 with an asterisk, which means that a good oral performance is expected given the extreme criticality of the written exam. This exam structure is reserved for students whose study plan includes only Module I (Machine Construction A, 6 credits), while for students who opt for Module II (Machine Construction AB, 12 credits), i.e. for the Design curriculum, learning will be assessed in a single final examination for Module II, for which it is (obviously) essential to be able to solve the exercises in Module I. IMPORTANT: For students under the previous teaching system (up to the academic year 24/25), in which only Machine Construction (9 CFU) appeared in the study plan, the examination methods and content remain unchanged (written test, passing grade 18/30, oral test).

sections.Learning objectives: TECNOLOGIA MECCANICA: This course provides the knowledge and ability necessary for analysis of manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. The primary objective of this course is to develop a level of proficiency sufficient such that students can understand mechanical production processes within an industrial context based on information provided within mechanical and detail drawings. To this end, acquisition of knowledge relating to the following points is necessary: - Information contained within a technical drawing in terms of component geometry, materials, surface finish and dimensional and positioning tolerances; - Issues relating to fulfilment of specific precision requirements during the production cycle and knowledge of measurement tools necessary for quantification; - Foundry and plastic deformation as primary forming processes; - Machining processes utilising machine tools; - Reversible and irreversible joining techniques. To this end, development of the following abilities is necessary: - Study of the primary forming processes of a component; - Determination of the raw material (in terms of dimensions, material and primary production process) for subsequent machining of a component; - Identification of the sequence of operations necessary to create the surfaces making up the component; - Referencing of the component with respect to machine tools utilising appropriate equipment; - Calculation of the forces acting throughout the cutting process and the power absorbed by machine tools. sections.Course unit content: The aim of this course is to study manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. A systematic approach aligned with process modelling is adopted for understanding the principles and mechanisms on which the manufacturing processes are based, and for understanding their capabilities and limitations in terms of achievable functional performance for specific manufactured products, systematic design and planning of the manufacturing process, and integration of the design and production processes. Modelling will be aimed at predicting the influence of process parameters on the resulting outcomes. The course content will be sufficiently analytical for an elementary university course and adequately descriptive for students that have no specific prior knowledge relating to manufacturing processes. The course will consist of lectures and tutorials where exercises will be completed together with the lecturer and discussion of industrial applications will take place.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: by means of frontal lessons, the student acquires the method and knowledge required to describe, understand and design the industrial production and storage systems, to define their maintenance criteria; student learns how to efficiently use project management tools by means of statistic basics provided. The student will learn the structure and the operating principle of industrial plants in terms of: organization and management of the transformation of raw material into finished product, reliability of complex systems, role of human resources and industrial automation, production flows and layout, KPI and performance measurements.Applying knowledge and understanding: Through practical classroom exercises connected to some important topics, students learn how to apply the acquired knowledge in a real context of design, as well as in multidisciplinary or non-familiar areas.In particular, the student will have to apply the acquired knowledge to the industrialization of a production process, starting from the feasibility study, defining the best production structure and management, assessing the possibility of using automated operations to replace manual ones and controlling process through KPIs.Making judgements: The student must be able to understand and critically evaluate the main production systems (forced and not-forced technological processes, production or assembly, manual or automated); using acquired knowledge, he will have to analyze existing systems and assess their performances and adequacy, assess the impact of strategic, planning and operational decisions, measure plant performances.Communication skills: Through the front lessons and the assistance of the teacher, the student acquires the specific vocabulary inherent to the production plants. At the end of the course, the student is expected to be able to communicate the main contents of the course, both written and orally, such as ideas, engineering issues and related solutions. The student must communicate his knowledge through appropriate tools, so numerical problems are solved using common methods in the industry such as tables, diagrams, flow charts, and numerical spreadsheets.Learning skills: The student who has attended the course will be able to deepen his knowledge of production plants through the autonomous consultation of specialized books, scientific or divulgative journals, even outside the topics explained during lectures.

sections.Course unit content: The course aims to provide the students with the general criteria for designing and realizing the main production plants, which are complex systems consisting of the technological plants, utilities and facilities that contribute to the achievement of the economic goal. Therefore, the content covered during the lessons in the first part of the course concerns the classification of production plants, with and without a constrained technological cycle, and manual and automated manufacturing and assembly processes. The main performance indicators for monitoring the efficiency of industrial plants are defined. Project management tools and reliability theory for the maintenance of production systems are also introduced. The second part of the course assesses the impact of automation on these processes, both from a control and predictive maintenance perspective, describes material handling and product storage systems, and introduces some methods for sizing storage systems.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and ability to understand: (I Dublin Descriptor) By the end of the course, the student will have developed and integrated his or her basic knowledge of metallic materials suitable for component fabrication using foundry and additive manufacturing technologies. He/she will have gained awareness of issues related to physical metallurgy, relationships between microstructure and mechanical properties of ferrous and non-ferrous alloys. In particular, by the end of the course the student will be able to select appropriate materials and heat treatments for engineering design. Skills: (II Descriptor: Ability to apply knowledge and understanding) Through lessons and in-class exercises related to all program topics, the student will learn how to apply the knowledge gained in a design context. Autonomy of judgment: (III, IV, V Dublin descriptor) The student should be able to critically understand the characteristics and behavior of matter by evaluating its properties and suitability in relation to the intended applications. He/she will also have to process the relevant data to verify the required performance. Communication skills: (III, IV, V Dublin descriptor) At the end of the course the student should have acquired sufficient language skills, at least as regards the specific technological terminology of the teachings.
sections.Full programme: Basic knowledge of physical metallurgy: Brief introduction to crystallography. Diffusion phenomena correlated to the main heat treatments: I° and II° Fick’s law. Defects within the metallic materials. Phase diagrams: basic characteristics, lever rule, cooling pathways at the thermodynamic equilibrium. Phase diagram of Fe-Fe3C and microstructures. Strengthening mechanisms of the metallic materials. Solidification in conventional and innovative processes. Mechanical characterisation: Tensile test, hardness test, and Charpy impact test. Innovative production process: Metal additive manufacturing: general description, applications and operation of the machine. Process parameters. Advantages and Disadvantages. Steel: Designation. The main microstructures obtained during the main industrial heat treatments. Heat treatments: quenching, annealing, tempering, normalizing. Nitriding and carburizing. Brief description of structural steels, special structural steels, tool steels, and stainless steels. Aluminium alloys: Designations. Main aluminium alloys: microstructure, mechanical properties and applications. Production of aluminium. Main heat treatments and effects induced by cold deformation. Additive Manufacturing. Analysis of application cases and selection criteria for metallic materials: During the course, various application cases will be presented, in which the selection of metallic materials will be carried out based on the required mechanical properties, the component’s function, and the choice of suitable treatments to meet specific operating conditions at room and high temperatures.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of this course the student should know the basics of machine design. He should be familiar with design schemes and checks required to analyze machine parts. Applying knowledge and understanding: He should be able to design a mechanical part on the basis of suitable material and process selection, load analysis and functional requirements. sections.Course unit content: The course covers the principles of mechanical design applied to machine components, starting with the strength characteristics of commonly used materials and the concept of safety. It then introduces methods and models for the schematization of acting loads and the calculation and sizing of components. A key aspect is the introduction to strength testing under fatigue loads. The course will cover the main mechanical components.
sections.Full programme: Introduction to Construction Design, Safety, Factor of Safety with Statistical Reliability Concepts, Technical Standards, Mechanical Testing of Materials, Tensile, Hardness, Impact, Fatigue, Fracture Testing, Metallic Materials (Steel, Cast Iron, Aluminum, Magnesium, Titanium Alloys), Non-Metallic Materials (Polymers and Ceramics), Manufacturing Technologies, Selection Criteria. Load Analysis, Equilibrium, Application of the Beam Model in Mechanics, Normal Force, Bending, Shear, and Torsion. Stresses and Strains. Mohr Circles. Principal Stresses, Strength Criteria (Tresca, Von Mises, Rankine), Ductility and Brittleness. Compressive Buckling and Eulerian Loading. Stiffness. Highly Curvatured Beams. Notched Geometries, Nominal and Local Stresses, Stress Concentration Factor Kt. Conformal and Non-Conformal Contact, Specific Contact Pressure, Hertzian Theory, Stresses in Contact between Elementary Bodies. Thermal Expansion. Fatigue of Metallic Materials, Characteristics of the Phenomenon, Fatigue Testing, Stress Limit fatigue, S/N curves, fatigue parameter estimates, influence factors, mean stress effect, fatigue damage accumulation, multiaxial stress effect, notch sensitivity, Notch effect factor Kf. Contact fatigue, pitting, fretting. Mechanical power transmission: axles and shafts, materials, construction details, sizing and testing, shaft-hub connections, gear wheels, pulleys; rolling bearings: types (rollers, balls) and load capacity, assembly, choosing bearings from the catalog; plain bearings: examples, materials, testing. Screws: examples and threads, testing. Loose connections: screws, bolts, rivets, and nails, standards for threaded parts, load transmission by shear or friction, bolted joints, preload, stiffness of parts and load distribution, testing in the presence of fatiguing loads, anti-loosening devices; pins. Fixed connections: welding: technical standards, sizing of welded joints, types of seams, strength testing criteria; notes on sizing of glued joints. Springs: fields of application, types, stiffness. sections.Learning objectives: TECNOLOGIA MECCANICA: This course provides the knowledge and ability necessary for analysis of manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. sections.Course unit content: The aim of this course is to study manufacturing processes, production systems and assembly methods for industrial components and products. A systematic approach aligned with process modelling is adopted for understanding the principles and mechanisms on which the manufacturing processes are based, and for understanding their capabilities and limitations in terms of achievable functional performance for specific manufactured products, systematic design and planning of the manufacturing process, and integration of the design and production processes. Modelling will be aimed at predicting the influence of process parameters on the resulting outcomes. The course content will be sufficiently analytical for an elementary university course and adequately descriptive for students that have no specific prior knowledge relating to manufacturing processes. The course will consist of lectures and tutorials where exercises will be completed together with the lecturer and discussion of industrial applications will take place.

sections.Full programme: 1. Curves. Preliminaries (linear algebra; polar coordinates and planar rotations). Parametric curves (velocity and acceleration; regular curves). Curve in polar coordinates. Length of a curve (curves in polar form; cartesian curves; piecewise regular curves). Repamareterization (cylindrical helix). Curvature and torsion. 2. Vector valued functions: continuity and limits. Real functions of two real variables (level sets). Polar, spherical, and cylindrical coordinates (vector valued functions). Elemens of topology. Integral of a function along a curve (curvilinear integral of functions and of vector fields; integral on the oriented boundary of planar sets). Quadratic forms (Sylvester criterion). Differentiable functions (infinitesimals and Taylor expansions; diﬀerential; maximum slope direction; total differential theorem; vector valued differentiable functions). Operations with partial derivatives. Higher order derivatives (Schwarz theorem; Taylor formula). Local extremes (Fermat theorem; nature of stationary points; sufficient conditions in two and three dimensions). Contrained extremes (Lagrange multipliers method in two variables). Surfaces in Euclidean space (Lagrange multipliers method in three variables). Potentials and curvilinear integrals (curl-free vector fields). 4. Multiple integrals. Integral over a rectangular box (reduction formulas for double integrals). Integration on a normal set. Change of variables (polar coordinates; an improper integral; implicit transformations). Integrals in three dimensions (integration by wires, integration by layers; change of variables). 5. Diﬀerential equations. Preliminar examples. Cauchy problem for equations and systems. Existence, extendability, and uniqueness of solutions. First order differential equations (first order linear equations; separable variable equations; Bernoulli equations). sections.Learning objectives: The module of PPLICAZIONI INDUSTRIALI ELETTRICHE aims at providing basic knowledge and methods for the analysis and synthesis of linear circuits in DC, AC and transient conditions. Part of the contents will be preparatory for later Electronics courses. The aim of the Electronics Elements module is to provide students with a basic knowledge of: - electronic components and circuits - analysis techniques of first and second order linear systems in the frequency domain - transfer functions and harmonic response functions - behavior and characteristics of feedback systems - techniques for evaluating the stability of linear systems 2) Ability to apply knowledge and understanding The skills that the student will be able to acquire with this teaching are: - analyze the behavior of linear systems, with particular reference to first and second order systems, through analysis in the frequency domain - analyze behavior and stability of feedback systems
sections.Prerequisites: The student must demonstrate familiarity with the basic teachings taught in the first years of the degree course. (Mathematical Analysis 1, Mathematical Analysis 2, General Physics 1, General Physics 2).
sections.Course unit content: The course aims to provide students with the general criteria for analyzing the behavior of basic electric and electronic circuits. Lectures will cover the following topics: Analysis and synthesis on linear electric circuits in direct current, alternating current, and transient operation. Energy analysis. Frequency analysis. Mathematical models of linear electronic devices and systems. Analysis of linear systems in the frequency domain in the frequency domain. Stability of feedback systems.
sections.Full programme: AIE: 1) Steady-state electrodynamics (6 hours). Voltage and currents. Resistor, voltage and current independent generators, Ohm's laws, energy. Voltage and current limits, rated values. Thermal sizing. Elements of Electronics: - Introduction to Electronics - Semiconductor Devices - BJT Linear Amplifiers - Laplace Transform and Transfer Function - Bode Plots - Passive Filters - Feedback Systems - Stability of Linear Systems - Operational Amplifier - Circuits with Operational Amplifiers - Overview of Power Converters - Exercises
sections.Bibliography: C.K. Alexander, M.N.O. Sadiku, G.Gruosso, G.Storti Gajani, "Circuiti elettrici, Sesta Edizione", McGraw-Hill libri Italia, 2022. ISBN9788838654909 G. Rizzoni, "Elettrotecnica. Principi e applicazioni", McGraw-Hill Education, 2018, ISBN9788838601293 A. Hambley, “Electrical Engineering: Principles and Applications”, 6th ed., Prentice Hall, ISBN-10: 027379325X
sections.Teaching methods: The ELECTRICAL INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS module includes lectures. In-class exercises will be completed by the instructor. The Electronics Elements module includes 3 training credits, which correspond to 24 hours of lessons. Teaching activities will be conducted by privileging frontal lessons alternating with classroom exercises. During the frontal lessons, the course topics will be addressed from a theoretical-design point of view, in order to promote a deep understanding of the topics and to bring out any prior knowledge on the topics in question by the trainees. The projected notes and any notes used to support the lessons will be uploaded to the Elly platform. To access this material, registration for the online course is required. Non-attending students are reminded to check the available teaching material and the instructions provided by the teacher via the Elly platform, the only communication tool used for direct teacher/student contact. The topics covered in class are indicated on this platform, which will then form the index of contents in view of preparing for the final exam.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The exam consists of a written test. The written test is unique for the two integrated modules of "Industrial Electrical Applications" and "Elements of Electronics". During the test, for the part of AIE, the student will have to demonstrate knowledge of circuit analysis and synthesis techniques in direct current, alternating current and transient operation, frequency analysis. For the part of Elements of Electronics, the student must demonstrate that he/she knows and can apply the techniques of analysis of linear systems covered in the course, and that he/she can analyze the behavior of simple circuits. Importance is given to the ability to solve exercises and answer simple theoretical questions.
sections.Other information: The teaching and support material for the lessons will be available on the Elly website.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of this course the student should know the basic phenomena of the classical electromagnetism and the underlying physical laws. Moreover, he should be able to resolve problems on the subjects treated in the theory lectures. Applying knowledge and understanding: The student should be able to analyze the electromagnetic phenomena and to interpret them on the basis of the mathematical formulation of the physical laws. Making judgments: By the end of the course, the student should be able to understand the physical phenomena of the electromagnetism. Communication skills: The student should be able to clearly present the basic concepts of electromagnetism and their consequences on observable phenomena. Learning skills: The student should have acquired the learning skills related to electromagnetism, which are necessary to undertake successive studies with a high degree of autonomy.
sections.Prerequisites: It is important to have an appropriate knowledge of classical mechanics and ondulatory phenomena as treated in the course of General Physics 1.
sections.Course unit content: The course is structured in two parts: theory and problems. The theory lectures cover the following subjects: - Coulomb's law and electric field - Gauss's law - Electric Potential - Conductors - Capacitance - Dielectrics - Current and resistance - DC circuits - Magnetostatics - Diamagnetism, paramagnetism and ferromagnetism - Electromagnetic induction - RL and LC circuits - Maxwell equations - Electromagnetic waves The problems are focused on the subjects treated in the theory part.
sections.Bibliography: G. Cantatore, L. Vitale, W. E. Gettys, Gettys Fisica 2: Elettromagnetismo - Onde. McGraw-Hill Libri Italia, Milano.
sections.Teaching methods: Slides will be used to convey the most important messages of the theory lectures. The problems will be resolved at the blackboard, possibly with the participation of the students. Slides and texts of the exercises are uploaded on the Elly platform before the corresponding lessons. Teaching activities will be in person.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The examination is based written tests, with exercises and theory questions. The written tests have a duration of two hours. Students can use a calculator. If the mark is at least 21/30, the examination is passed and an oral test is not required, but can always be requested to eventually improve the mark. If the mark is between 13 and 20/30, an oral test is compulsory to pass the examination. The eventual oral test focuses on the knowledge and understanding of the topics discussed during the lectures. The online registration is compulsory both for oral and written tests.
sections.Other information: Lectures attendance is highly recommended.

sections.Learning objectives: By means of the frontal lessons, the student should be independently able to understand and to schematize by means of mathematical models simple phisical phenomena involving particles and rigid bodies. Moreover, the student should acquire the aptitude to learn, with critical mind, the theachings typical of the Mechanical Engineering degree.
sections.Prerequisites: There are no mandatory propedeuticities, but Mathematical Analysis, Geometry and Phisics I are strongly recommended.
sections.Course unit content: Rational (or Theoretical) Mechanics is the science that studies the general laws of mechanical motions of material bodies (particles, rigid bodies) and establishes general procedures and methods for solving problems involving such motions. Being a mathematical science, Rational Mechanics deals not with real phisical objects but with abstract schematized conceptions. Consequently, Rational Mechanics il the link between the pure mathematics courses (Mathematical Analisys, Geometry) and the courses of engineering contents (expecially, Applied Mechanics). It is customary to divide the course into three basic parts: Statics (the study of the rules of composition of forces and the conditions of equilibrium of rigid bodies), Kinematics (the study of motions of bodies from the geometric viewpoint alone, without reference to the forces acting on the bodies) and Dynamics (the study of the relationships between the motions of material bodies and the forces acting on them) . In particular, we emphasize the plane kinematics of the rigid bodies, and the dynamics of the one-dimensional mechanical systems.
sections.Full programme: Free vectors theory - geometry of the plane curves - kinematics of the element - kinematics of the rigid body - relative kinematics - rigid plane motiond - polar curves - statics and dynamics of the element - cardinal equations - applied vectors theory - one-dimensional mechanical systems (Lagrange's equations) - statics and dynamics of the rigid body - statics and dynamics of the articulate systems.

sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The exam consists of twoo written tests and one possible oral test. The first written test (of 3 hours) contains one or more exercises. The students have to study the equilibrium position of a mechanical system (usually, two bodies) and to determine its motion equations. The utmost importance is given to the proceeding whereas the correctness of the numerical result it's not so important. The second written test (of 1.5 hours) will be held on 3/4 days after the first one. It consists of theoretical questions: definitions, properties, theorems, demonstrations,simple applications. A lot of examples of such written tests are available to students and shared on Elly platform. When the exam is exceeded , the student can decide to do also an oral test. The mark "cum laude" cam be acquired only after the oral test.

sections.Learning objectives: This course aims at teaching the fundamental knowledge for studying the functional and constructive features of mechanical devices, by means of drafted representations that comply with technical standards, and according to their choice as a consequence of the production process. The course goal is to provide students with the necessary awareness and knowledge to create and interpret technical drawings for both individual parts and assemblies. Specifically, students are expected to acquire the following fundamental skills:: (i) to understand the theory and basic notions of technical drawing and its related standards (ii) to know the main elements and modules of machines and mechanical systems (iii) to draft technical drawings based on their application and the manufacturing processes needed to realize the parts (iv) to compare design alternatives for mechanical systems based on external requirements (v) to develop adequate independence in the evaluation of mechanical systems for a correct design and representation (vi) to develop a fluency in the representation of mechanical systems (both in hand-sketching and with the help of software tools) (vii) to be able to provide new concepts and design solutions for components and assemblies considering the changing external requirements
sections.Prerequisites: None
sections.Course unit content: At the beginning of the course, there is an introduction to the basics of technical drafting, such as geometric constructions, orthogonal projections, axonometries, representations of surfaces, sections, rotations, and reflections. After some forewords about materials used in mechanical applications, metrology, and machining, this course thoroughly deals with typical issues of mechanical drafting, considering most used standards, conventional representations, and most common principles of dimensioning. Relationships with production and control processes are carefully taken into consideration. Further topics are dimensional tolerances, geometric tolerances, and surface roughness. There is a thorough analysis of separable joints (by means of threaded parts), fixed joints (welding, soldering), and elastic connections (by means of springs). Furthermore, couplings used for torque transmission from the shaft to other elements are analyzed (keys, cotter, splined shaft, pins). Other topics are bearings and seals, along with several application examples, with special emphasis on the methodology which lead to their choice and mounting. The course deals also with mechanical transmission devices, such as shafts, joints, belts, chains, and gears.
sections.Full programme: 1) Machine drawing basis: standards and standardization authorities, standard sizes of drawing sheets, basic line types and interpretation, font heights and types, drawing scales, sheet layout and title block, drawing types (assembly and part), bill-of-materials. 2) Axonometric projection: classification. Isometric, Dimetric, and Cabinet projections. 3) Isometric views: European system (first angle projection), American system (third angle projection). Symbols. Selection of Views. Designation and Relative Positions of Views. Development of Missing Views. Conventional representation. 4) Sectional views: definition, Conventional representation, Position of sectional views. Sectional view types: Full Section, Half Section, Local Section. Hatching of sections. 5) Dimensioning: definitions (dimension line, projection line, termination, value of the dimension). Special indications (Diameters, Chords, Archs, Angles, Radii, Chamfers, Tapered, etc.). Arrangement of dimensions (chain dimensioning, parallel dimensioning, combined dimensioning, co-ordinate dimensioning). Functional dimensioning, Technological dimensioning. Examples. 6) Materials and technologies: chipping, grinding, milling, refining, etc. Introduction to “Geometrical Product Specifications” (GPS). 7) Limits, Dimensional tolerances, and fits: Fundamental tolerances, Fundamental deviations, Method of placing limit dimensioning, Standards followed in industry (ISO), Fits (clearance, transition, interference). Indicating Dimensional tolerances on the drawings. Examples. 8) Geometrical tolerances: definitions. Tolerances of Form and Position. Indication of feature controlled. Indicating geometrical tolerances on the drawings. Examples. 9) Surface roughness: Introduction and definition. Surface roughness parameters. Indicating surface roughness on the drawings. 10) Screw thread and Screwed fasteners: Introduction and nomenclature, ISO thread series, Representation of threads. Bolted joints, Locking arrangements for nuts, Foundation bolts. 11) Shaft couplings: keys, Cotters, Pins, and Splined shafts. 12) Bearings and seals: Introduction and classification, Sliding contact bearings, Rolling contact bearings, Seals (o-ring, v-ring, rotary shaft seal, etc.).

In case the given time to complete the classroom assignment is not enough for the student, it is required to complete the assignment at home. Drawings produced during classroom exercises are part of the final exam and they must be provided to the teacher during the exam.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The exam consists of a writing assignment which lasts up to 3hours. The exam is characterized by 3 requests: (i) a technical drawing of an assembly (ii) a technical drawing of a component (iii) a set of 3 technical questions related to the topics investigated during the course The exam is conducted sequentially. The first part (2 hours and 30 minutes) is dedicated to completing the overall assembly drawing and the detailed drawing, while the second part (30 minutes) is dedicated to solving the 3 technical questions. The exam result (grade) is calculated by the teacher, considering the sum of the results obtained in the drawing part (overall assembly drawing + detailed drawing) and the technical questions. If the student wishes to take an oral exam (typically consisting of 2-3 questions related to the course topics), they can request it by emailing the teacher. The oral exam can result in an increase or decrease in the grade obtained from the written exam (and may also result in the student being failed). Access to the oral exam is granted only after passing the written test. The student must apply to the exam session by registering through the ESSE3 portal (open until 3 days before the scheduled exam date). The exam results are published on the ESSE3 portal within a week of the exam date. Students who did not pass the graphic drawing test can review their exam by scheduling an appointment with the teacher.

sections.Learning objectives: 1) Knowledge and understanding a) To know the basic theory of solid and structural mechanics b) To know and embrace the concepts of stress state, strain state, constitutive relationship c) To understand relations governing the internal action and the elastic curve of a beam d) To understand the response of beam elements under tension/compression, bending, shear, and torsion 2) Applying knowledge and understanding. To be able to: a) apply the basic concepts of solid and structural mechanics b) draw of the internal action diagrams for beams, for given load and constrain conditions c) evaluate the deflection of a beam, for given load and constrain conditions d) calculate the stress state of a beam subjected to tension/compression, bending, shear, and torsion e) calculate critical loads for compressed beams f) use the acquired knowledge for autonomously studying issues related to solid and structural mechanics 3) Making judgements a) to evaluate the applicability of structural models to describe real structures and elements b) to evaluate the applicability of the beam theory c) to assess and compare independently the engineering solutions of a structural problem d) choosing autonomously the right approach and the appropriate tools to solve a structural problem 4) Communication skills a) to communicate effectively in written and oral form in the context of solid and structural mechanics b) to know and know how to use the specific scientific / technical terminology of solid and structural mechanics c) to be able to properly use the mathematical language to describe the treated issues 5) Learning skill a) to catalog, schematize and elaborate the acquired knowledge b) to correlate the different topics one other and with the basic and related disciplines c) to autonomously use and apply the acquired knowledge
sections.Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of calculus, linear algebra and physics.
sections.Course unit content: The course aims to provide a unified treatment of the main aspects of the mechanical behavior of structures, in the linear elastic range. The first part of the course is devoted to the evaluation of the static schemes and strain in elastic solids under assigned external actions. Structural theories for beams will subsequently be addressed. The topics covered are more specifically as follows. • Basic principles of mechanics. Fundamental equations of statics. • Constraints, Free Body Diagrams, calculation of constraint reactions. • Shear force and bending moment diagrams in slender beams. • Stress and strain. Linear elastic constitutive relation. Mohr’s graphical representation. Strength criteria. • De Saint Venant problem. Normal stress. Twist. Simple bending. Shear. • Solution of statically undetermined structures. • Instability phenomena, Euler beam. The application aspect is taken care of through the introduction of a large number of solved examples and exercises.
sections.Full programme: Principles of rigid body mechanics: Forces and moments, Systems of forces, Distributed loads, Constraints and constraint reactions Forces and moments transmitted by beam elements: Beam element concept, Forces and moments transmitted by beams, Calculation of internal stress resultants, Differential equilibrium equations Stress, strain, and constitutive relations: Stress analysis, Strain analysis, Constitutive relations, Yield criteria Beams under axial load: The semi-inverse method by de Saint-Venant, The semi-inverse method for beams under axial load Beams under bending: Area geometry, Bending of symmetric cross-sections, Eccentric axial load Beams under torsion: Torsion of circular cross-sections, Torsion of rectangular cross-sections, Torsion of thin-walled closed sections, Torsion of composite sections Beams under shear: Shear stresses on horizontal planes, Shear stresses along arbitrary chords, Shear center Deflections of bent beams: Elastic curve equation, Example cases, Notable cases and superposition method, Solution of hyperstatic structures Buckling of compressed beams: Euler's formula for simply supported beams, Other constraint conditions, Design of beams under buckling load
sections.Bibliography: - F. P. Beer, E. R. Johnston, J. T. DeWolf, D. F. Mazurek, “Meccanica dei solidi. Elementi di scienza delle costruzioni”, McGraw-Hill - Course notes
sections.Teaching methods: We provide lectures and exercises on the blackboard. As a rule, lectures will follow as much as possible the recommended text, so that the student can critically review what has been developed in the classroom. From time to time, homework exercises will be assigned; clarification will be given during office hours. The teaching material will be uploaded on Elly platform weekly.
sections.Assessment methods and criteria: The exam is based on a written test, where the student will be asked to solve a few exercises of the same type as those carried out in the classroom during lectures, and to answer an open-ended question. During the written test, the student can use calculator and formulary. The evaluation is on 0-30 scale.

sections.Learning objectives: Knowledge and understanding: At the end of this course the student should know the main theoretical and applicative aspects of Fluid Mechanics. Moreover, he should gain understanding of the techniques of analysis of the problems in Fluid Mechanics, paying attention to the differences between models and real behavior of the physical processes. Applying knowledge and understanding: The student should be able to describe the physical process by using applied mathematics; to select the parameters and the variables involved in the process; to solve the most common applicative cases checking the results with engineering approach. Making judgments: By the end of the course, the student should be able to evaluate the reliability of the simplified models or the need to adopt advanced models. Communication skills: The student should be able to clearly present the results of the analysis, in oral or written form, also by means of tables and charts.
sections.Prerequisites: Differential analysis, Geometry, Rational Mechanics, Physics.
sections.Course unit content: The course provides the students with the basic knowledge of Fluid Mechanics in the context of Classical Mechanics. The students shall be able to solve the main technical problems related with the interaction between fluids and structures and with pressurized flow. Numerical exercises about the topics listed in the program will be developed.
sections.Full programme: Introduction to vector fields and to differential operators, to tensors. Dimensional analysis. Fluids and fluid behaviour. Definition of fluid as a continuum. Fluid mechanics variables and units of measurement. Fluid properties. Stresses in a continuum. Fluid statics. Internal stresses in fluids at rest. Differential analysis of fluid statics. Finite control volume analysis of fluid statics. Pressure distribution in incompressible fluids. Pressure measurement. Hydrostatic force on plane and curved surfaces. Buoyancy. Fluid kinematics. Lagrangian and Eulerian approach. Velocity and acceleration fields. Total derivative. Pathlines, streamlines, streaklines. The Reynolds transport theorem. Flow regimes. Basic fluid dynamics. Differential and finite control volume analyses of a fluid flow. Basic laws of Fluid Mechanics. Conservation of mass. Continuity equation. The linear momentum equation. Dynamic load of a flow. The differential equation of linear momentum. Frictionless flow. The ideal fluid model. Euler equation. The Bernoulli equation. Physical and geometrical interpretation. Examples of the use of the Bernoulli equation. Gradually varied flow. Extension of the use of the Bernoulli equation to streams. Flow of viscous fluids. The viscous fluid model. The Navier-Stokes equations. Analytical solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations: Couette flow, Hagen-Poiseuille flow. Flow in ducts. Laminar and turbulent regimes. Equations of motion. Reynolds number. Continuous and minor losses. Resistance laws. Moody chart. Pipe flow problems.

sections.Learning objectives: 1) Knowledge and understanding a) To know the basic theory of solid and structural mechanics b) To know and embrace the concepts of stress state, strain state, constitutive relationship c) To understand relations governing the internal action and the elastic curve of a beam d) To understand the response of beam elements under tension/compression, bending, shear, and torsion 2) Applying knowledge and understanding. To be able to: a) apply the basic concepts of solid and structural mechanics b) draw of the internal action diagrams for beams, for given load and constrain conditions c) evaluate the deflection of a beam, for given load and constrain conditions d) calculate the stress state of a beam subjected to tension/compression, bending, shear, and torsion e) calculate critical loads for compressed beams f) use the acquired knowledge for autonomously studying issues related to solid and structural mechanics 3) Making judgements a) to evaluate the applicability of structural models to describe real structures and elements b) to evaluate the applicability of the beam theory c) to assess and compare independently the engineering solutions of a structural problem d) choosing autonomously the right approach and the appropriate tools to solve a structural problem 4) Communication skills a) to communicate effectively in written and oral form in the context of solid and structural mechanics b) to know and know how to use the specific scientific / technical terminology of solid and structural mechanics c) to be able to properly use the mathematical language to describe the treated issues 5) Learning skill a) to catalog, schematize and elaborate the acquired knowledge b) to correlate the different topics one other and with the basic and related disciplines c) to autonomously use and apply the acquired knowledge
sections.Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of calculus, linear algebra and physics.
sections.Course unit content: The course aims to provide a unified treatment of the main aspects of the mechanical behavior of structures, in the linear elastic range. The first part of the course is devoted to the evaluation of the static schemes and strain in elastic solids under assigned external actions. Structural theories for beams will subsequently be addressed. The topics covered are more specifically as follows. • Basic principles of mechanics. Fundamental equations of statics. • Constraints, Free Body Diagrams, calculation of constraint reactions. • Shear force and bending moment diagrams in slender beams. • Stress and strain. Linear elastic constitutive relation. Mohr’s graphical representation. Strength criteria. • De Saint Venant problem. Normal stress. Twist. Simple bending. Shear. • Solution of statically undetermined structures. • Instability phenomena, Euler beam. The application aspect is taken care of through the introduction of a large number of solved examples and exercises.
sections.Full programme: Principles of rigid body mechanics: Forces and moments, Systems of forces, Distributed loads, Constraints and constraint reactions Forces and moments transmitted by beam elements: Beam element concept, Forces and moments transmitted by beams, Calculation of internal stress resultants, Differential equilibrium equations Stress, strain, and constitutive relations: Stress analysis, Strain analysis, Constitutive relations, Yield criteria Beams under axial load: The semi-inverse method by de Saint-Venant, The semi-inverse method for beams under axial load Beams under bending: Area geometry, Bending of symmetric cross-sections, Eccentric axial load Beams under torsion: Torsion of circular cross-sections, Torsion of rectangular cross-sections, Torsion of thin-walled closed sections, Torsion of composite sections Beams under shear: Shear stresses on horizontal planes, Shear stresses along arbitrary chords, Shear center Deflections of bent beams: Elastic curve equation, Example cases, Notable cases and superposition method, Solution of hyperstatic structures Buckling of compressed beams: Euler's formula for simply supported beams, Other constraint conditions, Design of beams under buckling load
